title: Taco on Friday, pizza on Saturday
sentences: Before, we didn't decide that much, or in the eighties the kids didn't decide everything, but they do today,
so it's kind of like taco on Friday and pizza on Saturday in like ninety percent of Norwegian homes, I think.
No wiggle room — if you try something else there's crying — but it wasn't like that at our place.
Mum decided the menu, and we often had homemade lasagne, sometimes moussaka too,
because she holidayed in Greece and picked up some ideas there — tzatziki and, yeah, stews that had been simmering a long time, that kind of thing.
She brought a bit with her from the seventies, right — she came from that kind of lefty milieu really,
so there was this Spanish beef stew and that kind of thing they kind of brought with them from the seventies.
They made red wine themselves on the bathroom floor in a big tank, you know.
And it always smelled of yeast and whole baked trout,
I mean, she — because today it's salmon fillets, there wasn't much of that back then.
She'd buy a whole fish, cut it open and put in butter and garlic and parsley and that sort of thing, and Hasselback potatoes baked in aluminium foil.
So the weekend was really something special,
and I also remember that she — and this was a bit the Dynasty era too, right,
so even though we were lefties we still watched that kind of thing,
so that whole shift to dressing up for dinner — we started doing that in the eighties.
On Fridays we'd take a bath in the tub and then get clean,
and then my sister and I were allowed to go and put on something nice,
and then come downstairs all dressed up for this meal that was timed for half past six of course, so we could sit and eat in front of the TV,
watch the half-six news and eat — it was just wonderful.
Yes.
I really recognise that, and especially that half-hour thing — that's what you had for weekday dinners,
there was like half an hour — it had to be ready by then and everyone was starving,
and then you had to get going — and it was also about lifting the weekend dinners up a notch.
And I also remember when you were younger, it was a bit like you'd end up staying for dinner at someone else's place,
you'd go home with someone after school and then just stay there until dinner time,
and it was always really exciting to see what other people ate.
And I just want to — actually a digression, but it just occurred to me,
someone said now it's going to be spaghetti and mince for dinner — and that's exactly what it was.
It was boiled-to-death mince and — no, boiled-to-death spaghetti and fried mince,
and there was no spice, no sauce, nothing.
I remember I was completely shocked.
Do any of you have any memories of eating at other people's places, where — yes.
Well, I can say one thing about exactly that — eating at other people's.
I had a friend whose family I think had a bit more money because they got things early,
so they had a microwave very early, and they had a pantry that was always full of stuff you could just help yourself to.
It wasn't like that at our house — it wasn't just free-for-all — but I remember us being there,
but it was a bit sad compared with today, and maybe people have a bit more to spend.
At that time it was like if you were at someone's house
when it was dinner time, it wasn't certain you'd be invited to that dinner.
No.
It was quite often that you had to go sit in the bedroom and wait, and that, like.
In the bedroom, yes.
